To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the degradation of nanostructured porous materials in vivo can be predicted from the in vitro degradation in the absence of ROS in the media.
nanostructured porous silicon undergoes enhanced degradation when exposed to reactive oxygen species, which is upregulated in the tumour environment.

(i) PSi undergoes accelerated erosion in the presence of reactive oxygen species, which are upregulated in diseased tissues, (ii) the in vivo and in vitro degradation kinetics of PSi correlate when the same conditions are applied in vitro as in vivo (ROS-containing medium).
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding and predicting the behaviour of nanostructured materials in complex biological environments.
the development of a nanostructured silicon drug carrier for the controlled release of anticancer drugs in the neoplastic tissue.
the development and application of nanotechnology for cancer treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the in vivo degradation of nanostructured PSi is governed by the ROS levels in the surrounding environment.

nanostructured PSi is a biocompatible, biodegradable and biologically active material that can be programmed to deliver drugs in a controlled and sustained manner, with the potential to be applied in the clinic.

in vivo degradation kinetics of nanostructured porous Si in neoplastic tissue is determined by the balance between ROS-mediated oxidation of Si and ROS-scavenging by the Si scaffold, and is independent of the initial PSi porosity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PSi drug carriers degrade faster in the diseased state than in the healthy state.
PSi degradation is a function of the local microenvironment and that this can be exploited for the controlled release of drugs from PSi in vivo.
PSi degradation can be controlled by the surrounding environment, and this can be used to modulate drug release in vivo.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of ROS-containing media in vitro is a suitable model to predict the in vivo performance of PSi drug carriers in neoplastically altered tissues.
PSi can be used as an effective drug delivery system in the diseased tissue, as its degradation is significantly faster than in healthy tissues.

the use of nanostructured porous materials for drug delivery in diseased tissues should be carefully considered and that the use of such materials for drug delivery should be accompanied by the use of ROS scavengers to avoid the premature degradation of these materials.
